big: Two corporate bond funds sit in the same SEBI category. One shows a yield of 9% and the other 7.5%. The gap is not a gift from a cleverer manager. Something is being paid for.

lines: This fund shows 9% yield but my friend's shows 7.5%. Same category. Why?
Same category does not mean same risk. First see how the market prices a rating, then what the extra yield really buys.

alt: Five bars of made-up yields rising as the rating falls from AAA to BBB
caps: Rating agencies grade bonds. AAA is the strongest, then AA+, AA, A, BBB, and below.
The market asks a higher yield as the grade falls. These yields are made up.
A BBB issuer must pay about 5 points more than a AAA issuer to attract lenders.
The extra yield is not a bonus. It is payment for the chance of a missed payment.

alt: Fund X yields 7.5 percent, Fund Y 9 percent; one written-off holding wipes out years of extra income
caps: Fund Y holds lower-rated bonds and yields 9.0%. Fund X holds mostly AAA bonds and yields 7.5%.
Y earns 1.5% a year more. After three years that is 4.5% of extra income.
But if a 5% holding is written off, the loss is 5% of the fund, in either fund.
Y needs about 3.3 years of extra yield to repay one such loss. And Y is likelier to have one.

h: A downgrade hits the price first
alt: Four bars of a bond price falling through two downgrades and a default
caps: A 3-year bond with a 9% coupon, rated AA, is priced at ₹100.
Cut to A: buyers now want 11%, so the price falls to about ₹95. No payment has been missed.
Cut again to BBB: they want 14%, and the price is about ₹88. The issuer is still paying.
Then it defaults. If 40% is recovered, the bond is worth about ₹40.
Prices fall on downgrades, long before any default. The NAV shows it as it happens.

q: Rohan's friend's corporate bond fund yields 7.5% and his own shows 9%. Same SEBI category, similar maturity. What should Rohan check first?
opts: The credit table, to see how much sits in lower-rated papers
The expense ratio, since a lower fee explains most of a 1.5% gap
The last month's return, since a higher yield shows up there
Whether the plan is direct or regular, since cost sets the yield
why: The gap usually comes from credit quality. The credit table shows how much sits in AAA and how much in lower grades.
Expense ratios differ by a fraction of a percent. A 1.5% gap in portfolio yield points to what the bonds are, not the fee.
One month of returns also reflects price moves, and says little about which bonds the fund holds or why it yields more.
Plan type changes cost by a small amount. The portfolio yield on the factsheet is the same for both plans.

q: A fund holds a 4% position in a bond rated AA. Today the agency cuts it to A. No coupon has been missed. What is the likely effect?
opts: No effect, since the issuer is still paying, so the price holds
The fund must sell the bond immediately at its original price
Its price usually falls now and the NAV dips, before any default
The fund cannot report the change until a payment is missed
why: Prices react to the downgrade itself. The market wants a higher yield for the added risk, so the price falls.
A forced sale at the old price cannot happen. The market sets the price, and buyers will pay less after a cut.
Buyers price in the higher risk straight away, so the price drops on the news, and the NAV marks it down that day.
Funds mark holdings to market daily and disclose ratings. They do not wait for a missed payment to show a cut.

q: A fund earns 1.8% a year more than a high-quality rival. It holds 4% in one issuer, which defaults with nothing recovered. About how many years of the extra yield does it take to repay that loss?
opts: About 0.5 years, since one default is a rounding error
None, because diversification removes credit risk entirely
About 4 years, the same number as the 4% loss
About 2.2 years, since 4% divided by 1.8% a year
why: The loss is 4% of the fund, which is much larger than half a year of the 1.8% extra yield.
Spreading across issuers reduces credit risk but cannot remove it. A default still costs the fund its share.
Treating 4% as 4 years ignores the 1.8% yearly extra. Divide the loss by the extra yield instead.
A 4% loss at 1.8% a year takes about 2.2 years of extra yield to repay. Diversification limits this but does not remove it.

q: A client says a AAA rating means her debt fund cannot lose money. What is the honest reply?
opts: Ratings are opinions that can be cut, and AAA prices still move
Correct, since AAA bonds are guaranteed by the rating agency
AAA applies only to government bonds, whose prices never move
The rating is irrelevant, because the coupon is what decides returns
why: AAA means the lowest credit risk, not none. A rating can be cut, and even AAA bond prices fall when rates rise.
Rating agencies grade risk. They do not guarantee payment or compensate holders if an issuer fails.
AAA is a grade given to company issuers. Even government bond prices move when yields change.
The coupon is only part of it. A downgrade or default can change the price and hit NAV whatever the coupon was.

pts: Higher yield usually means more credit risk. The extra yield pays for the risk.
A downgrade cuts the price before any default, and it shows in NAV.
Diversification reduces credit risk, it does not remove it. Read the credit table.
